newsitem.title: USA: SEC moves to ease access to U.S. capital markets.
newsitem.headline: SEC moves to ease access to U.S. capital markets.

text.p: The Securities and Exchange Commission Tuesday voted unanimously to reduce the time investors must hold privately offered securities before reselling them to the public.

The revision allows for the resale of limited amounts of restricted securities by anyone to one year instead of the current two years and unlimited amounts by non-affiliates of the company after a two-year period instead of three.

The commission also proposed revisions to three rules that will allow investors easier access to capital markets. The adopted rule becomes effective at the end of April and the comment period for the three proposals also end in April.

"These initiatives will directly benefit small companies, which despite their role as an engine of economic growth -- sometimes face unnecessary impediments in raising capital," SEC Chairman Arthur Levitt said at an open commission meeting.
The commissioners proposed eliminating longstanding restrictions on trading volume that have prevented investors from selling all of their private placement holdings at once.
For the first time since the rule was adopted in 1972, the threshold would rise to 1,000 shares or $40,000 sale price test from 500 shares or $10,000.
The agency also moved to cut off abuses of Regulation S, the agency's rule first adopted in 1990 exempting U.S. corporations from registering offshore offerings
Proposed changes will lengthen the holding period to two years from 40 days in which U.S. companies relying on Reg S "safe harbor" may not sell equities to U.S. investors.
"This was a great first step," said Marc Morgenstern, managing partner of Kahn, Kleiman, Yanowitz & Arnson Co L.P.A. and an expert on securities.

"I think that the conjunction of making the holding periods for restricted securities the same under both rule 144 and Regulation S is a very positive regulatory approach," Morgenstern told Reuters in a phone interview.

The same security with the same characteristics should be subject to the same economic consequences and they accomplished that, he said. "And one can only ask whether or not a shorter holding period, perhaps six months, would be appropriate."
Shortening the holding periods for unregistered securities offered in private placements is part of an agency effort to make it easier for companies to raise capital.

The shorter holding period should shrink the discounts that companies have to pay investors who buy these securities, translating into a direct cost savings for these companies, Levitt told the meeting.
The so-called "private placement" of securities allows issuers to avoid registering them as long as they are being sold to investors who have agreed not to resell them for a specified period of time.

The commission also proposed changes to give small companies the same "rapid" access to capital markets as larger companies that register offering on a "shelf" -- selling stock on a delayed basis -- if certain conditions are met.
